This page accompanies Chapter 9. The simulation runs locally in the browser
through WebR; no classroom installation of R is needed.

## Random assignment with imperfect compliance

The population contains never-takers, compliers, and always-takers. There are
no defiers, so monotonicity holds. Treatment effects are heterogeneous and
treatment receipt is endogenous.

```{webr}
library(ivreg)

set.seed(5280)
n <- 4000
Z <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
type <- sample(
  c("never", "complier", "always"),
  n,
  replace = TRUE,
  prob = c(0.25, 0.55, 0.20)
)

D0 <- as.integer(type == "always")
D1 <- as.integer(type %in% c("complier", "always"))
D <- ifelse(Z == 1, D1, D0)

U <- rnorm(n)
tau <- 1 + 0.7 * (type == "complier") + 0.4 * U
Y0 <- 0.5 + U + rnorm(n)
Y <- Y0 + D * tau

table(type, Z, D)
```

## Build the Wald estimator from its two ITTs

```{webr}
outcome_itt <- mean(Y[Z == 1]) - mean(Y[Z == 0])
first_stage <- mean(D[Z == 1]) - mean(D[Z == 0])
wald <- outcome_itt / first_stage
true_late <- mean(tau[type == "complier"])

c(
  outcome_itt = outcome_itt,
  first_stage = first_stage,
  wald = wald,
  true_late = true_late
)
```

The Wald estimate should be close to the mean effect for compliers, not
necessarily the population ATE.

## Compare IV and OLS

```{webr}
fit_iv <- ivreg(Y ~ D | Z)
fit_ols <- lm(Y ~ D)

summary(fit_iv, diagnostics = TRUE)
summary(fit_ols)
```

Try lowering the complier probability and rerun the whole page. The first
stage becomes weaker, the IV ratio becomes more variable, and the usual normal
approximation becomes less trustworthy.
